thread:
jess: Heads-up: our replay vs synthetic bench divergence is bigger than expected. Replay p95 is consistently lower but CPU is higher. I dug into client behavior and kernel traces; looks multi-factor.

matt: Can you list the harness configs side-by-side? we need to rule out simple client differences.

jess: Synthetic harness: vegeta-style clients, no explicit keepalive, pool size default, TCP_NODELAY not set. Replay: captured upstream client with persistent conns, TLS session reuse, and HTTP/2 multiplexing for gRPC calls. Commands: 
```
vegeta attack -targets=targets.txt -rate=200 -duration=60s
# replay tool used recorded-order playback with original conn ids
```

sara: Big ones: HTTP/2 vs HTTP/1.1 head-of-line + connection churn, TLS full-handshakes/sec, and Nagle causing tiny write delays. Also check ALPN and session ticket reuse.

alex: From server pprof and perf: high conn churn -> more kernel context switches, futex waits, and expensive SSL_accept paths. When we see many ephemeral TLS sessions, user->kernel cycles spike and tail latency moves up.

jess: Also KV cache: the replay preserves real prefix correlation so hit-rate falls for certain prompts. Our synthetic ran normalized prompt lengths which accidentally inflated cache hit-rate and reduced per-token compute.

matt: So to be systematic: (1) match client protocol and ALPN settings, (2) match pool sizes + keepalive + TCP_NODELAY, (3) force TLS session reuse behavior to be equivalent, (4) align prompt/token length distro and request ordering, (5) warm KV cache or measure warm vs cold separately, (6) collect batch-size histograms and kernel profiles.

ci-bot: benchmark-run: id=bf-2026-03-17-99, p50=34ms, p95=198ms, cpu=78%, kv_hit=60% (raw-synthetic)

sara: Note on batching heuristics: small changes in request ordering change how continuous-batching groups requests. That can flip which kernels are selected (fused vs unfused attention), altering both latency and CPU. Capture per-request batch_id and batch_size histograms.

alex: Quick profiling tip: record both user-space pprof and kernel perf events (context switches, syscalls/sec, softirq), and collect OpenSSL/boringssl stats for session reuse and expensive key ops.

jess: I ran tuned-synthetic with increased pool size, keepalive enabled, and TCP_NODELAY set. p95 reduced from 198ms -> 176ms, CPU slightly up. Still slightly above replay. Batch histogram shows replay had more micro-batches of size 3-4, synthetic formed mostly 1-2.

matt: Run plan: three experiments: (A) bad-synthetic (single-conn-per-request), (B) tuned-synthetic (match client networking + tcp options), (C) replay (captured ordering). For each record: p50/p95, kv_hit, open_conns/sec, tls_handshakes/sec, avg_conn_lifetime, batch_size_hist.

sara: I'll run a microbench toggling TCP_NODELAY and measuring tail for small payload writes to quantify Nagle impact.

alex: If tuned-synthetic still diverges, we should suspect kernel scheduling or batching-induced kernel selection differences. Also consider HT vs non-HT CPU pinning effects and NUMA locality.

jess: Added conn churn and TLS-handshake counters to harness. Uploading tuned logs next. ETA 25m.

matt: After we confirm, we'll add an "apples-to-apples benchmarking" doc to eng-runtime explaining the checklist + instrumentation. If there's a regression, file perf ticket with artifacts.

jess: Uploaded artifact: s3://redwood-bench/bf-2026-03-17-99/artifacts.zip (includes pprof, perf, batch histograms, conn metrics).

alex: :thumbsup: Good instrumentation. Let's avoid assuming synthetic is always conservative; misconfigured synthetic can be optimistic.

ci-bot: benchmark-artifact uploaded: s3://redwood-bench/bf-2026-03-17-99/artifacts.zip
